name: Teatro Español
overview: Public theatre owned by Madrid City Council, at Calle del Príncipe 25 on the Plaza de Santa Ana (Spanish Wikipedia; theatre website; El Español).

Origins: a decree of Philip II in 1565 set up the Cofradía de la Sagrada Pasión in Madrid with a space for staging plays; the brotherhood bought the Calle del Príncipe site in 1582, opened its playhouse on 21 September 1583 and sold it to the City Council 32 years later (Spanish Wikipedia).

Earlier names: the Corral del Príncipe became the Teatro del Príncipe with a new building of 1735 to 1745 by Juan Bautista Sachetti and Ventura Rodríguez, and took the name Teatro Español by royal decree in 1849 (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Teatro Español: public: Madrid City Council through its company Madrid Destino

name: CAC Málaga
aliases: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo de Málaga
overview: The contemporary art centre of the city of Málaga, now named MUCAC Mayoristas after its merger with the MUPAM into MUCAC (Agencia memorandum 2026).

Since September 2024 its management has been entrusted to the Agencia Pública para la Gestión de la Casa Natal de Pablo Ruiz Picasso y Otros Equipamientos Museísticos y Culturales (Agencia memorandum 2026).
What is there: the pages read did not state a collection size.
funding_verdict: CAC Málaga: public, funded by the Ayuntamiento de Málaga through a municipal agency.

name: Centre Pompidou Málaga
overview: An outpost of the Centre Pompidou in El Cubo, a building of 6,300 square metres between quays 1 and 2 of the port of Málaga, with a coloured glass cube by Daniel Buren over its entrance (Málaga City Council, 11 July 2024; The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024).

Málaga City Council and the Centre Pompidou signed the first contract on 3 September 2014 and the centre opened in March 2015; the deal was renewed early in 2018 and again in July 2024 for 28 March 2025 to 27 March 2035 (Málaga City Council, 11 July 2024; The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024).

What is there: it has no collection of its own. The contract brings six semi-permanent exhibitions of 20th and 21st century art from the Centre Pompidou's collection over the decade, two temporary exhibitions a year, a jointly curated show within the Hors Pistes festival and a yearly workshop exhibition for young visitors (Málaga City Council, 11 July 2024). More than a million visitors had come by July 2024, by the Centre Pompidou's count (The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024).
funding_verdict: Centre Pompidou Málaga: public, paid by Málaga City Council, which also pays yearly fees to the Centre Pompidou in Paris
wider_context: The Art Newspaper sets the renewal beside the Centre Pompidou's other paid partnerships: New Jersey withdrew promised funding for a Jersey City branch in June 2024, a Seoul branch is planned in the Hanwha group's Tower 63, and the Pompidou signed a deal in 2023 with Saudi Arabia's Royal Commission for AlUla (The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024).

The same article reports a Cour des comptes warning of a 'high risk of slippage in terms of costs and deadlines' in the Paris building's renovation, which closes the Paris site for five years from 2025 (The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024).

name: Museo Carmen Thyssen Málaga
overview: A museum in Calle Compañía 10, Málaga, run by the Fundación Palacio de Villalón, registered in the Andalusian foundations register as number 1,248 of 2010 (Plan de Actuación 2026).

The foundation's statutes give as purposes signing the loan contract for the Colección Carmen Thyssen Bornemisza, keeping and exhibiting it, and receiving the municipal buildings the Ayuntamiento de Málaga assigns to it (Plan de Actuación 2026).

What is there: the permanent collection is made up entirely of works from the Colección Carmen Thyssen, lent free of charge, with more than 180 works of Spanish and especially Andalusian painting of the 19th and early 20th century and a small selection of older masters from the 13th to 18th centuries (Plan de Actuación 2026).
funding_verdict: Museo Carmen Thyssen Málaga: mixed, a city guarantee plus tickets, shop and corporate sponsors.

name: Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo
aliases: C3A Centro de Creación Contemporánea de Andalucía (Córdoba site)
overview: The Andalusian regional centre for contemporary art, in the Cartuja de Santa María de las Cuevas on the Isla de la Cartuja, Seville, with a second site, the C3A, in Córdoba (CAAC website).

Created in February 1990 by the Junta de Andalucía; the Cartuja monastery became its seat in 1997, when the Conjunto Monumental de la Cartuja and the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Sevilla and their collections joined it; the C3A and the Pabellón del Siglo XV were added in 2018 (CAAC website).

The collection starts in the mid 1950s and runs to the present, with attention to Andalusian art in relation to Spanish and international art; the pages read did not give a number of works (CAAC website).
funding_verdict: Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo: public, an agency of the Junta de Andalucía

name: Museo Nacional de Escultura
overview: State museum of Spanish sculpture on three sites in Valladolid: the Colegio de San Gregorio, the Palacio de Villena and the Casa del Sol with its annex, the church of San Benito el Viejo (museum website).
It grew out of the provincial fine arts museum set up in 1842 in the Colegio de Santa Cruz with art taken from convents after Mendizábal's 1836 nationalisation of church property (museum website).
The Second Republic made it a national museum in 1933 under its present name and moved it to the Colegio de San Gregorio (museum website).
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Escultura: state-funded: Spain's Ministry of Culture

name: Artipelag
overview: Artipelag is an exhibition venue at Hålludden on Värmdö, about 30 minutes from Stockholm, with a 9,000 sq. m exhibition hall (museum website; The Art Newspaper, 1 March 2012).
Björn Jakobson, founder of BabyBjörn, first envisioned it in 2000 with his wife Lillemor and it opened in 2012; the Artipelag Foundation has owned it since 2022 (museum website).

What is there: no permanent collection is described. Jakobson said in 2012 that the founders had no collection of their own and wanted to show art in the natural setting; permanent works named are the rock formation in Bådan and Bigert & Bergström's Solar Egg (The Art Newspaper, 1 March 2012; museum website).
funding_verdict: Artipelag: private, founder wealth now held in a foundation

name: Ájtte, Swedish Mountain and Sámi Museum
overview: Sweden's main museum of Sámi culture and a specialist museum of the nature and culture of the mountains, at Kyrkogatan 3 in Jokkmokk (ajtte.com).

A foundation formed in 1983 runs it; a smaller museum that had existed in Jokkmokk since 1965 was merged into the new building, and the museum opened in June 1989 with eight times the floor space (ajtte.com).
Ájtte means storage hut in Sámi, and the museum describes itself as a store that keeps things for the future (ajtte.com).
funding_verdict: Ájtte: public foundation: Swedish state, Norrbotten Region, Jokkmokk Municipality and two Sámi organisations

name: Moderna Museet Malmö
overview: Moderna Museet Malmö is a modern art museum at Ola Billgrens plats 2–4 in Malmö; the page shows the orange facade of the building (museum website).
It opened in December 2009 as a three-party arrangement between the City of Malmö, Region Skåne and the Swedish state through Moderna museet (annual report 2023).

What is there: the museum website gives the collection as 140,000 works of modern and contemporary art, Swedish and international; 84,331 unique works were registered in the museum's art database at the end of 2023, and 306 works were acquired in 2023, all by donation or foundation funds (museum website; annual report 2023).
funding_verdict: Moderna Museet Malmö: mainly public, state appropriation plus city premises

name: Fondation de l'Hermitage
overview: The Fondation de l'Hermitage is an art museum in a nineteenth-century manor house in a park above Lausanne, at Route du Signal 2 (Lausanne Tourisme).
The pages read did not state when it opened; the city's Préavis 2026/46 says it has held a major place in fine arts for 40 years.
What is there: two or three major exhibitions a year, often Impressionists and others such as Degas and Gauguin, and a permanent collection of Chinese porcelain in the basement (Lausanne Tourisme).
funding_verdict: Fondation de l'Hermitage: a foundation whose house is being renovated with City of Lausanne credits and patron money

name: Fondation Pierre Gianadda
overview: Museum and cultural centre at Rue du Forum 59 in Martigny, Valais, with temporary exhibitions, a Gallo-Roman museum, a car museum, a sculpture park and a concert season (foundation website; Swiss commercial register).

Founded by the engineer Léonard Gianadda in memory of his brother Pierre, who died in a plane crash on 31 July 1976; the deed was signed on 24 February 1977 and the museum opened on 19 November 1978, Pierre's 40th birthday (foundation website, history page).

Site: in June 1976 a Gallo-Roman temple was found where Léonard planned a 16-storey tower block; the ruins are shown in the central space (foundation website). The building is in Gard stone and concrete, in a 7,000-square-metre park (Universalis).
funding_verdict: Fondation Pierre Gianadda: founder-built foundation, run on its own income and sponsors, with public officials on its board

name: Shedhalle (Rote Fabrik)
overview: Institution of contemporary and critical art at Seestrasse 395, 8038 Zürich, inside the Rote Fabrik, a compound in the city that has been in use as a culture and recreation centre since the early 1980s (Shedhalle).
It evolved in 1986 from an interest group of local artists who felt under-represented in the established art system (Shedhalle).

The Rote Fabrik is a former industrial complex by Lake Zürich. The Standard Telephon und Radio AG left the Wollishofen site in 1972 and the city bought it. The city opened it as a provisional cultural centre in 1980 and 1981 and voters approved a culture and leisure centre there in 1987 (SRF, 12 March 2020).
funding_verdict: Shedhalle: City of Zurich and Canton of Zurich funds, with private foundations for projects

press_items.title: Barnaby Drabble, "We Want Everything: Assembled Thoughts on Artist-led Culture in Zürich" (Fillip 4, Fall 2006)

name: Jim Thompson House Museum
overview: The former Bangkok home of James H.W. Thompson, kept as a museum with guided tours in Thai, English, French, Chinese and Japanese (museum website).
It holds Thompson's Asian art collection; the page gives no object count or opening year.
Archive: not mentioned on the page read.
funding_verdict: Jim Thompson House Museum: funding not stated on the page read

name: Zeugma Mosaic Museum
overview: Mosaic museum on Hacı Sani Konukoğlu Boulevard in the Şehitkamil district of Gaziantep, built on the site of a former tobacco factory (Turkish Museums, Ministry of Culture and Tourism; Daily Sabah).
It opened on 9 September 2011 (Daily Sabah; Wikipedia).
Holds finds from Zeugma on the Euphrates, where rescue excavations began in 1998 and revealed Roman villas with mosaics (Daily Sabah).
funding_verdict: Zeugma Mosaic Museum: state: Turkey's Ministry of Culture and Tourism

name: Sakıp Sabancı Museum
overview: A museum of calligraphy, painting and decorative arts in the Atlı Köşk, a villa at Emirgan on the Bosphorus in Istanbul, with a modern gallery annex (museum website).

Prince Mehmed Ali Hasan of the Egyptian Khedive family commissioned the villa in 1925 from the Italian architect Edoardo De Nari; Hacı Ömer Sabancı bought it in 1951, the Sabancı family gave it with its collections and furnishings to Sabancı University in 1998, and it opened to the public in 2002, with a further extension in 2005 (museum website; Sabancı University).

The collection has four parts: the Arts of the Book and Calligraphy, from the fourteenth to the twentieth century, begun with the purchase of a calligraphic panel by Sultan Mahmud II and enlarged in the 1980s by buying private collections; a Painting Collection begun by Sakıp Sabancı in the 1970s, from Ottoman-era to Republican painting; Furniture and Decorative Arts begun by the Khedive family and enlarged by the Sabancı family; and 22 stone archaeological pieces in the gardens (museum website). The museum's Google Arts & Culture page lists 435 items online, 81 of them by Abidin Dino, with Osman Hamdi Bey, İbrahim Çallı, Nazmi Ziya Güran and Fikret Mualla among the painters.
funding_verdict: Sakıp Sabancı Museum: private, paid for by the Sabancı group and university, plus sponsors and tickets

name: Alserkal Avenue
overview: A cluster of 90 warehouses in Al Quoz, Dubai, with over 70 galleries, visual and performing arts organisations, designers and entrepreneur-led businesses (Alserkal press release, November 2020).
Founded in 2007 by Abdelmonem Bin Eisa Alserkal; the first galleries opened in late 2007 (The National, 16 June 2014).
What is there: commercial galleries and arts organisations, not a collection; Ayyam, Carbon 12 and Gallery IVDE were there from the beginning (The National, 16 June 2014).
funding_verdict: Alserkal Avenue: private, family-owned property with a family foundation.

name: Etihad Museum
overview: A 25,000 square metre museum complex including the restored Union House, on Jumeirah Road, Dubai (The National, 5 January 2017).

Designed by Moriyama and Teshima Architects; inaugurated by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid on 2 December 2016, 45th National Day, and open to the public the following January (The National, 5 January 2017).
What is there: old passports, personal items such as rings, eyeglasses and pocket watches, stamps and letters; no counts were given (The National, 5 January 2017).
funding_verdict: Etihad Museum: public, run by the Dubai Culture & Arts Authority; no amounts found.

name: The Burrell Collection
overview: A museum in Pollok Country Park on the south side of Glasgow, with free entry, in a building designed by Gasson, Andresen and Meunier (commissioned in 1972) and refurbished by John McAslan + Partners (museum website; Glasgow Life, 29 March 2022).

Sir William Burrell and his wife Constance gave the collection to the City of Glasgow in 1944; following their wish for a countryside setting it opened in Pollok Country Park in 1983 (museum website).

What is there: about 9,000 objects: Chinese art, described as one of the most significant holdings in the UK; medieval stained glass, arms and armour; more than 200 tapestries and about 150 carpets, including the Wagner garden carpet; and late 19th-century French paintings with more than 20 works by Degas, Manet's Roses in a Champagne Glass (1882) and Cézanne's The Chateau of Medan (1879 to 1880) (museum website; Glasgow Life, 29 March 2022).
funding_verdict: The Burrell Collection: mainly public, Glasgow City Council through Glasgow Life, with lottery and government capital grants

name: The Royal Standard
overview: Artist-led studio and gallery complex at 5 Mann Street, Baltic Triangle, Liverpool. It calls itself "Liverpool's oldest and largest artist-led studio and gallery" and "home to Liverpool's largest community of artists."
Founded in 2006 in a small pub in Dingle by four Liverpool-based artists (the Royal Standard's about page; The Skinny, 1 June 2016).

In 2008 it moved to a larger industrial space on Vauxhall Road and relaunched for the Liverpool Biennial 2008. It moved to the Northern Lights site in Cains Brewery in 2017 because of "a precarious rolling contract" at Vauxhall (The State of the Arts, Devon Forrester-Jones, 21 March 2017).
funding_verdict: The Royal Standard: small public and lottery grants: Arts Council England and National Lottery Community Fund grants, with donations

press_items.title: C. James Fagan, "'It's my dream job, but it's voluntary': Trials And Triumphs At The Royal Standard" (11 May 2016)

name: The NewBridge Project
overview: Artist-led studio, gallery and bookshop at the Shieldfield Centre, 4-8 Clarence Walk (via Stoddart Street), Newcastle upon Tyne. It describes itself as "an artist-led space that supports artists, curators and communities."

Established in 2010. In 2015 it occupied a 29,000 square foot office block in the city centre, offered affordable studios to early-career artists and had around 80 studios, a large exhibition space and an independent bookshop (Corridor8, Niomi Fairweather, 4 October 2015).
Registered as a charity (no. 1173849) and a company (no. 10582100), registered 18 July 2017 (Find that Charity).
funding_verdict: The NewBridge Project: mixed public and charitable: Arts Council England, Newcastle City Council, trusts and the university
